Living together for a long time, two kids - young and older. I was in my thirties when we had the first one, partner was slightly older. They wanted kids, they thought there was more to life. I grew up in a big family and always thought I'd have kids, but never felt like we were ready. Realised that I'd never feel ready and that I wanted them, so it was as good a time as any. First year was amazing. Cut back to fewer days a week work, one solid day looking after the baby each work week, and it was fantastic. Second year, major depression (work burnt me out and the kid just didn't sleep). Third year, the next one comes. At this point I realised that all the time I was thinking it was hard having a single kid, you've got no idea how hard it is until you have 2. (Have heard that 3 is even harder then with 4+ you've got the game mechanic sorted out, the engine ticking over nicely, and it all gets easier.) Anyway, decided that 3 is just going to be too expensive (we like being able to afford holidays). I've got to tell you, having kids is a blast. It's hard work. They take time, energy and money. Each Saturday and Sunday morning is spent taking the kids around to various commitments they have. Then, twice a week in the evenings, one of us is out of the house until 8-9pm taking the daughter to her dancing. Spare time ~~and spare money~~ is effectively nil. (Re-reading this, I realise that they don't drain all our money. Yes, I'm not buying a new computer every year, but we are taking a couple of week long road trips every year around my home country and fly back to the states at least every second year.) But I fucking love it. Watching them come up with their own observations on the world is fantastic and seeing them develop their own mental model of how the world works is an absolute delight to behold. It's hard listening to my daughter jabber on. She makes up the most fantastical stories. Talks for fucking hours and, much to my disgust, takes her books into the toilet. My son has a much more technical mind. The partner is often out for work (higher paying executive role) in the evenings or interstate for business, the kids just pull their shit together and we operate the household like a well-oiled machine. There's bedlam and there's laughs. There are tears and there are smiles. It is that bad and it is that good. With kids, the gamut of life expands. You lose time, but you gain joy. You lose the luxury of being self centered, but you gain a steadfast knowledge that you'd give your life for theirs. They teach you a new dimension of love and bring another dimension of happiness. You know that you're going to make decisions that now involve a lot of compromise, but others are going to be thinking of you. I guess what I'm trying to say is this: they change your life, they don't end it. How you adapt to that change is the telling of how you're going to be as a parent. Good luck! :)
